children.name: Artiodactyla
Delphinidae
Globicephala
children.description: Pilot whales are medium-sized oceanic dolphins known for their distinctive bulbous heads and jet-black coloration. They are highly social animals that travel in tight-knit family groups called pods, often containing 20-100 individuals. These intelligent marine mammals are found in deep offshore waters throughout the world's oceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pilot whales can be distinguished from other dolphins by their prominent rounded foreheads (called melons) and their uniformly dark coloration. They are also notably larger than most other dolphin species, with adults reaching 12-24 feet in length.
children.funFact: Pilot whales are among the few animals besides humans that experience menopause, with older females living decades beyond their reproductive years to help care for their grandchildren and share knowledge with the pod.

children.name: Tursiops
children.description: Bottlenose dolphins are medium-sized marine mammals known for their distinctive bottle-shaped snouts and curved dorsal fins. These highly intelligent cetaceans are among the most recognizable dolphins, with robust bodies that can reach 8-12 feet in length. They are social animals that live in pods and are famous for their acrobatic abilities and complex behaviors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bottlenose dolphins can be distinguished from other dolphin species by their pronounced, elongated rostrum (snout) that resembles a bottle, along with their relatively large size and distinctive falcate (curved) dorsal fin.
children.funFact: Bottlenose dolphins have signature whistles that function like names - each individual develops a unique whistle that other dolphins use to call them, much like humans use names to identify each other.

children.name: Delphinus
children.description: Common dolphins are medium-sized marine mammals known for their distinctive hourglass or crisscross color pattern along their sides. They are highly social animals that travel in large pods and are among the most acrobatic of all dolphin species, frequently leaping and riding waves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Common dolphins can be identified by their unique yellowish or tan hourglass-shaped patches on their sides, which distinguish them from other dolphin species that typically have simpler color patterns.
children.funFact: Common dolphins can form massive superpods containing thousands of individuals, making them one of the most gregarious marine mammals in the world.

children.name: Leucopleurus
children.description: Leucopleurus is a genus containing just one species of oceanic dolphin found in the North Atlantic. These are medium-sized dolphins known for their distinctive white and yellow patches along their sides, which give them their common name of Atlantic White-sided Dolphin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dolphin genera, Leucopleurus dolphins have a unique color pattern with bright white and yellowish patches on their flanks that create distinctive side stripes.
children.funFact: Atlantic White-sided Dolphins are incredibly social and often travel in pods of hundreds or even thousands of individuals, making them one of the most gregarious dolphin species in New England waters.

children.name: Grampus
children.description: Grampus is a genus containing just one species - Risso's dolphin, a distinctive marine mammal found in deeper ocean waters. These dolphins are known for their robust build and unique scarred appearance that develops as they age.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dolphins, Risso's dolphins have a blunt, square-shaped head without a prominent beak and develop extensive white scarring across their bodies from social interactions and encounters with squid.
children.funFact: Risso's dolphins are born dark gray but gradually turn almost completely white as they accumulate scars throughout their lives, making older individuals appear ghostly pale in the water.

children.description: Oceanic dolphins are highly intelligent marine mammals with streamlined bodies, prominent beaks, and distinctive dorsal fins. They are active swimmers that live in social groups called pods and use echolocation to navigate and hunt for fish and squid in open ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other whale families, oceanic dolphins have pronounced beaks, cone-shaped teeth, and are generally smaller in size. They also tend to be more acrobatic and social than their larger whale relatives.
children.funFact: Oceanic dolphins have individual signature whistles that work like names, allowing them to identify and call to specific members of their pod even in murky water.

children.name: Balaenopteridae
Balaenoptera
children.description: Balaenoptera whales are large baleen whales known for their streamlined bodies and distinctive throat pleats that expand when feeding. These rorqual whales are among the fastest and most agile of all baleen whales, capable of incredible bursts of speed when hunting or traveling. All three New England species are filter feeders that gulp enormous amounts of water and prey, then push the water out through their baleen plates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other baleen whales, Balaenoptera whales have numerous throat pleats (called ventral pleats) that allow their mouths to expand dramatically when feeding. They also have tall, curved dorsal fins set far back on their bodies and relatively pointed heads.
children.funFact: The fin whale, a member of this genus, is the second-largest animal on Earth and can reach speeds of up to 25 mph, earning it the nickname 'greyhound of the sea.'

children.name: Megaptera
children.description: Megaptera is a genus containing just one living species - the magnificent humpback whale. These are large baleen whales known for their incredibly long pectoral fins, which can reach up to one-third of their total body length. Humpback whales are famous for their complex songs, acrobatic breaching behaviors, and epic migrations between feeding and breeding grounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Humpback whales are easily distinguished from other baleen whales by their exceptionally long pectoral fins and distinctive bumpy head covered in tubercles (knobs). They also have a more robust body shape and unique black and white coloration patterns on their tail flukes.
children.funFact: Each humpback whale has a unique pattern on the underside of its tail fluke, like a fingerprint, which scientists use to identify and track individual whales throughout their lives.

children.description: Rorquals are the largest group of baleen whales, including some of the biggest animals ever to live on Earth. These massive marine mammals filter-feed by taking enormous gulps of water and prey, then pushing the water out through their baleen plates while keeping the food inside. They're known for their distinctive throat grooves that allow their mouths to expand dramatically when feeding.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rorquals can be distinguished from other baleen whales by their pleated throat grooves and their streamlined body shape built for speed. Unlike right whales, they have a prominent dorsal fin and are much more agile swimmers.
children.funFact: A blue whale's mouth can hold up to 80 tons of water and food - that's more than the weight of most adult blue whales themselves!

children.name: Bovidae
Bos
children.description: The genus Bos includes the true cattle - large, heavy-bodied mammals with cloven hooves and complex four-chambered stomachs for digesting grass and other plant material. These powerful herbivores are characterized by their sturdy build, prominent horns (in most species), and ability to thrive on grasslands and pastures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bos cattle are distinguished from other bovines by their larger size, more massive build, and distinctive skull structure with horns that curve outward and upward from the sides of the head.
children.funFact: Domestic cattle can recognize and remember over 100 individual faces of other cattle, and they form complex social hierarchies within their herds.

children.name: Ovis
children.description: Sheep are domesticated mammals belonging to the genus Ovis, characterized by their woolly coats and grazing lifestyle. They are ruminants with four-chambered stomachs that allow them to efficiently digest grasses and other plant materials. All members of this genus are hoofed animals with a stocky build and typically curved horns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sheep can be distinguished from goats by their woolly (rather than hairy) coats, their tendency to flock together more tightly, and their generally more docile temperament. Their tails hang down rather than standing upright like goats.
children.funFact: Sheep have excellent memories and can recognize up to 50 individual faces of other sheep for over two years, helping them maintain complex social relationships within their flocks.

children.name: Capra
children.description: Goats are medium-sized mammals in the cattle family known for their sure-footed climbing abilities and adaptability to harsh environments. They are herbivores with four-chambered stomachs that allow them to digest tough plant materials, and both males and females typically have horns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Goats can be distinguished from sheep by their upright tails, beards (especially in males), and straighter hair rather than wool. They also have a more independent and curious nature compared to their sheep relatives.
children.funFact: Goats have rectangular pupils that give them nearly 360-degree vision, helping them spot predators while grazing on steep mountainsides.

children.description: Bovids are a large family of hoofed mammals that includes cattle, sheep, goats, antelopes, and buffalo. All members of this family are ruminants, meaning they have four-chambered stomachs that allow them to digest grass and other tough plant materials by chewing their cud. Both males and females typically have hollow, unbranched horns that grow continuously throughout their lives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike deer which shed their antlers annually, bovids have permanent horns made of keratin (the same material as fingernails) covering a bony core. Their horns are never branched and continue growing throughout the animal's lifetime.
children.funFact: Bovids are incredibly diverse, ranging from tiny dikdiks that weigh just 7 pounds to massive Cape buffalo that can weigh over 1,900 pounds!

children.name: Cervidae
Odocoileus
children.description: Odocoileus is a genus of medium-sized deer found throughout North and Central America. These deer are characterized by their brownish coats, white undersides of their tails, and the males' branching antlers that are shed and regrown each year. They are highly adaptable animals that thrive in forests, fields, and suburban areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other deer by their moderate size, distinctive tail markings (either white underneath like white-tailed deer or black-tipped like mule deer), and their relatively large ears. Unlike elk or moose, Odocoileus deer have more compact builds and smaller antlers.
children.funFact: White-tailed deer can leap up to 10 feet high and 30 feet in length, and can run up to 40 miles per hour when escaping predators.

children.name: Alces
children.description: True Moose (Alces) is a genus containing the largest members of the deer family, characterized by their massive size and distinctive broad, flattened antlers found on males. These impressive animals are perfectly adapted for life in northern forests and wetlands, where they browse on aquatic plants and woody vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moose are distinguished from other deer by their enormous size (up to 1,500 pounds), their uniquely shaped palmate antlers that spread out like giant hands, and their long legs that allow them to wade deep into water.
children.funFact: A bull moose's antlers can span up to 6 feet across and weigh up to 40 pounds, yet they shed and regrow this massive bone structure every single year!

children.description: Deer are graceful, hoofed mammals that belong to the family Cervidae. They are herbivores that feed on leaves, twigs, fruits, and other plant materials, and are well-adapted for running and jumping through forests and open areas. Most deer species are known for their keen senses and their ability to leap great distances when startled.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets deer apart from other hoofed mammals is that males (and in some species, females) grow antlers made of bone that are shed and regrown each year. Unlike horns, which are permanent and made of keratin, antlers start as soft, blood-filled tissue called velvet before hardening into solid bone.
children.funFact: A male deer's antlers can grow up to an inch per day during peak growing season, making them one of the fastest-growing tissues in the animal kingdom!

children.name: Phocoenidae
Phocoena
children.description: Typical porpoises in the genus Phocoena are small, robust marine mammals with triangular dorsal fins and spade-shaped teeth. They are among the smallest cetaceans, typically measuring 4-6 feet in length, and are known for their shy, elusive behavior around boats. These porpoises prefer shallow coastal waters and are often found in harbors, bays, and estuaries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike dolphins, typical porpoises have blunt, rounded snouts rather than elongated beaks, and their teeth are flattened and spade-shaped instead of conical. They also tend to be smaller and more stocky than most dolphins.
children.funFact: Harbor porpoises are one of the few marine mammals that can echolocate at ultrasonic frequencies above human hearing range, using clicks up to 150 kHz to navigate and hunt in murky coastal waters.

children.description: Porpoises are small, stocky marine mammals that belong to the whale and dolphin family. They have compact, torpedo-shaped bodies with triangular dorsal fins and distinctive spade-shaped teeth, unlike the cone-shaped teeth of dolphins. These intelligent creatures are excellent swimmers that feed primarily on fish and squid in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Porpoises can be distinguished from dolphins by their smaller size, blunt rounded heads without prominent beaks, and characteristic triangular dorsal fins. They also tend to be more shy and elusive than their dolphin relatives.
children.funFact: Porpoises communicate using high-frequency clicks and whistles that are often too high-pitched for humans to hear without special equipment.

children.name: Balaenidae
Eubalaena
children.description: Right whales are massive baleen whales known for their stocky, robust build and distinctive callosities - raised patches of rough skin on their heads. These gentle giants are slow-moving filter feeders that strain tiny copepods and other small organisms from the water using their long baleen plates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Right whales lack a dorsal fin and have a deeply curved mouth that gives them a distinctive bow-shaped jawline. Their heads are covered with unique patterns of callosities that are as individual as fingerprints.
children.funFact: Right whales got their name because whalers considered them the 'right' whale to hunt - they swim slowly, float when killed, and contain large amounts of valuable oil and baleen.

children.description: Bowhead and right whales are among the largest baleen whales, known for their massive heads that can make up one-third of their body length. These gentle giants are filter feeders that use their long baleen plates to strain tiny organisms like copepods and krill from the water. They are slow-moving whales that spend most of their time near the surface, making them historically easy targets for whalers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other baleen whales, members of this family lack a dorsal fin and have distinctively arched upper jaws that give them their characteristic curved mouth shape. Their baleen plates are exceptionally long and fine, allowing them to filter very small prey.
children.funFact: North Atlantic right whales are so critically endangered that each individual whale has been named and photographed, with scientists able to identify every whale by the unique pattern of rough skin patches called callosities on their heads.

children.name: Suidae
Sus
children.description: The genus Sus includes the true wild boars and warty pigs, robust omnivores known for their intelligence and adaptability. These stocky mammals have elongated snouts perfect for rooting through soil and forest floors in search of food, and they're found across diverse habitats from woodlands to grasslands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sus are characterized by their prominent, mobile snouts, coarse bristly hair, and in many species, distinctive facial 'warts' or protuberances. Unlike other pig families, they have relatively long legs and a more streamlined body shape adapted for running through dense vegetation.
children.funFact: Wild boars have an incredible sense of smell that's about 2,000 times more sensitive than humans, allowing them to detect truffles and other food sources buried up to three feet underground.

children.description: Suids are the true pigs, including wild boars, domestic pigs, and various species of wild pigs found around the world. These sturdy mammals are known for their snouts, which they use for rooting through soil to find food, and their omnivorous diet of roots, fruits, insects, and small animals. They're highly intelligent and social animals that live in family groups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Suids have distinctive pig-like snouts with a flat, disc-shaped tip that's perfect for digging, along with a stocky build and relatively short legs. Unlike other pig-like animals, true suids have four toes on each foot and typically lack the complex stomach chambers found in other hoofed mammals.
children.funFact: Wild boars can run up to 25 miles per hour and are excellent swimmers, capable of swimming to islands several miles offshore.

children.name: Physeteridae
Physeter
children.description: True sperm whales are the largest toothed whales in the ocean, characterized by their massive, block-shaped heads that can make up one-third of their total body length. These deep-diving giants are perfectly adapted for hunting squid in the ocean's depths, with powerful sonar abilities and the largest brain of any animal on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other whales, true sperm whales have a single blowhole located on the left side of their head rather than on top, and their enormous head contains a waxy substance called spermaceti that was once highly valued by whalers.
children.funFact: Sperm whales can dive deeper than 3,000 feet and hold their breath for over 90 minutes while hunting for giant squid in the ocean's darkest depths.

children.description: True Sperm Whales are massive marine mammals known for their enormous, square-shaped heads that can make up one-third of their total body length. These deep-diving whales are found in oceans worldwide and are famous for their ability to dive to extraordinary depths in search of their favorite prey, giant squid.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True Sperm Whales are distinguished from other whale families by their distinctive block-shaped heads filled with a waxy substance called spermaceti, and their single blowhole located on the left side of their head rather than on top.
children.funFact: Sperm whales can hold their breath for up to 90 minutes and dive deeper than 7,000 feet, making them one of the deepest-diving mammals on Earth.

children.name: Kogiidae
Kogia
children.description: Kogia is a genus of small sperm whales that includes the pygmy sperm whale and dwarf sperm whale (though only the pygmy sperm whale is found in New England waters). These compact marine mammals are much smaller relatives of the famous giant sperm whale, typically reaching only 8-11 feet in length. They are deep-diving whales that feed primarily on squid and small fish in offshore waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their massive sperm whale cousin, Kogia whales have a distinctive shark-like appearance with a small, squared-off head and a false gill slit behind each eye. They also have a much smaller spermaceti organ and a more curved, dolphin-like dorsal fin.
children.funFact: When threatened, pygmy sperm whales can release a cloud of reddish-brown intestinal fluid to confuse predators, similar to how squid release ink!

children.description: Dwarf and pygmy sperm whales are small, deep-diving whales that are much smaller relatives of the famous giant sperm whale. These compact marine mammals have square-shaped heads and prefer deep ocean waters where they hunt for squid and deep-sea fish. They are among the most elusive whales in our waters, rarely seen at the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their massive sperm whale cousin, these whales are quite small (8-12 feet long) and have a distinctive shark-like dorsal fin. They also have a unique ability to expel a cloud of reddish-brown intestinal fluid when threatened, similar to how a squid releases ink.
children.funFact: These whales can dive to depths of over 1,000 feet and hold their breath for up to 45 minutes while hunting for squid in the dark depths of the ocean.

children.name: Ziphiidae
Mesoplodon
children.description: Mesoplodont beaked whales are a group of deep-diving marine mammals known for their distinctive elongated snouts and preference for deep ocean waters. These medium-sized whales are among the most mysterious cetaceans, spending most of their time in the deep sea where they hunt for squid and deep-water fish. They are rarely seen at the surface and are considered some of the least understood whales in the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mesoplodont beaked whales are distinguished from other beaked whales by their relatively small size and the unique tooth arrangements in males, with most species having only one or two pairs of teeth that often protrude from the lower jaw in unusual positions.
children.funFact: These whales are so elusive that some species have never been seen alive - they're only known from specimens that have washed ashore, earning them the nickname 'ghost whales' among marine biologists.

children.description: Beaked whales are deep-diving marine mammals known for their distinctive elongated snouts or 'beaks' and their elusive nature. They are among the most mysterious whales, spending most of their time in deep ocean waters where they hunt for squid and deep-sea fish. These medium-sized whales are rarely seen at the surface, making them some of the least understood cetaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other toothed whales, most beaked whale species have only one or two pairs of teeth that often don't emerge until adulthood, and in many species only males develop visible teeth. They also have a unique throat groove pattern and can hold their breath for exceptionally long periods during deep dives.
children.funFact: Beaked whales are the champion deep divers of the mammal world, with some species capable of diving over 9,800 feet deep and staying underwater for more than two hours.

children.name: Monodontidae
Delphinapterus
children.description: Belugas are a unique genus of Arctic whales known for their distinctive white coloration and bulbous, rounded heads called melons. These medium-sized toothed whales are highly social marine mammals that live in cold northern waters. The genus contains only one living species, making belugas quite special in the whale family tree.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other whales, belugas are pure white as adults and lack a dorsal fin, having only a low ridge along their backs. They also have extremely flexible necks that allow them to turn their heads in all directions, unlike most other whale species.
children.funFact: Belugas are sometimes called 'white whales' or 'sea canaries' because they're among the most vocal of all whales, producing a wide variety of clicks, whistles, and chirps to communicate with each other.

children.description: The Monodontidae family includes two of the most distinctive Arctic whales: narwhals and belugas. These medium-sized whales are perfectly adapted to life in icy polar waters, with thick blubber and specialized features that help them navigate frozen seas. Both species lack the prominent dorsal fin found in most other whales, making it easier to swim under ice.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other whales, monodontids have no dorsal fin and possess extremely flexible necks that allow them to turn their heads. They also have unique teeth - belugas have simple peg-like teeth while narwhals famously have a single spiral tusk.
children.funFact: Belugas are the only whales that can change their facial expressions, thanks to their flexible facial muscles and unfused neck vertebrae that allow them to nod and turn their heads.

children.description: This diverse order includes all whales, dolphins, and porpoises, as well as land mammals like deer, cattle, pigs, and their relatives. Despite looking very different, these animals share a common ancestor and have similar bone structures in their limbs and specialized digestive systems. The group's name comes from the even number of toes (usually two or four) found on the feet of the land-dwelling members.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group have a unique ankle bone called an astragalus that has pulley-like grooves on both ends. Most also have complex, multi-chambered stomachs that help them digest plant material efficiently.
children.funFact: Whales and dolphins are more closely related to hippos and pigs than they are to other marine mammals like seals - their flippers actually contain the same finger bones found in hoofed animals!

children.name: Carnivora
Mustelidae
Neogale
children.description: New World Weasels are a group of sleek, carnivorous mammals native to the Americas. These agile predators share a characteristic long, slender body shape and short legs that make them excellent at pursuing prey through tight spaces like burrows and dense vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their Old World cousins, New World weasels evolved separately in the Americas and have distinct genetic lineages. They tend to be larger on average than European weasels and show unique adaptations to New World environments.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Neogale' literally means 'new weasel' - these species were only recently recognized as being genetically distinct enough from European weasels to deserve their own genus in 2021.

children.name: Lontra
children.description: New World River Otters are semi-aquatic mammals perfectly adapted for life in and around freshwater systems. These playful carnivores have streamlined bodies, webbed feet, and dense waterproof fur that keeps them warm while swimming and diving for fish, frogs, and other aquatic prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their Old World cousins, New World River Otters have longer, more tapered tails and slightly different skull structures. They're also generally more solitary than some other otter species, though they can be quite social during mating season.
children.funFact: River otters can hold their breath for up to 8 minutes underwater and have special muscles that can close their ears and nostrils while diving!

children.name: Pekania
children.description: Fishers are medium-sized carnivorous mammals in the weasel family, known for their dark brown fur and cat-like appearance. They are skilled climbers and hunters that live primarily in dense forests, despite their name having nothing to do with catching fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fishers are larger and more robust than other weasels like martens, with longer legs and a bushier tail. They have a distinctive pointed face and are one of the few predators capable of successfully hunting porcupines.
children.funFact: Fishers are one of the only animals that can kill porcupines by repeatedly attacking their face and flipping them over to access their unprotected belly.

children.name: Mustela
children.description: Typical weasels (Mustela) are small, agile carnivorous mammals with elongated bodies and short legs that make them perfectly suited for hunting in tight spaces. These skilled predators have dense fur coats that often change color seasonally, helping them blend into their surroundings throughout the year.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other mustelids by their extremely slender build, relatively small size, and their ability to undergo dramatic seasonal color changes from brown summer coats to white winter pelage.
children.funFact: Typical weasels can squeeze through any opening larger than their skull, allowing them to pursue prey like voles and mice directly into their underground burrows and tunnels.

children.name: Martes
children.description: Martens are sleek, cat-sized members of the weasel family that are perfectly adapted for life in the trees. These agile carnivores have semi-retractable claws and flexible ankles that allow them to climb headfirst down tree trunks, making them exceptional arboreal hunters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Martens are distinguished from other weasel family members by their tree-climbing abilities, bushy tails, and relatively large size. They have longer legs and more cat-like proportions compared to their ground-dwelling cousins like fishers or weasels.
children.funFact: American Martens can rotate their hind feet nearly 180 degrees, allowing them to descend trees headfirst like a squirrel despite being carnivores.

children.description: Mustelids are a diverse family of carnivorous mammals known for their elongated bodies, short legs, and incredible agility. These skilled predators include weasels, otters, fishers, and martens, all of which have dense fur coats and strong, musky scents produced by special glands. Most mustelids are excellent hunters with sharp teeth and claws, though they vary greatly in size from tiny weasels to robust fishers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mustelids have characteristically long, flexible bodies with short limbs, making them perfectly adapted for pursuing prey into tight spaces like burrows and tree hollows. They also possess prominent scent glands that produce strong odors for communication and territory marking.
children.funFact: Despite their name, fishers rarely eat fish and are actually one of the few predators capable of successfully hunting porcupines by flipping them over to attack their unprotected belly.

children.name: Canidae
Canis
children.description: The genus Canis includes wolves, dogs, and their close relatives - medium to large-sized carnivores with long snouts, pointed ears, and bushy tails. These intelligent pack animals are highly adaptable and can thrive in diverse habitats from wilderness areas to suburban neighborhoods. All members of this group are capable of interbreeding and share similar social behaviors and hunting strategies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Canis species have longer legs and more elongated skulls compared to foxes, and typically hunt in coordinated groups rather than alone. Their vocalizations include howling, which is rare among other canids like foxes.
children.funFact: Domestic dogs and coyotes can interbreed to produce fertile offspring called 'coydogs,' though this rarely happens in the wild due to different mating seasons and behaviors.

children.name: Vulpes
children.description: Typical foxes are small to medium-sized canids known for their pointed snouts, large ears, and bushy tails. They are highly adaptable predators that hunt small mammals, birds, and insects, and are famous for their intelligence and cunning behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Vulpes are distinguished from other fox genera by their relatively small size, triangular ears, and elongated snouts that are proportionally longer than those of wolves or domestic dogs.
children.funFact: Red foxes have incredible hearing and can detect the sound of a mouse squeaking from up to 100 feet away, allowing them to hunt prey even under deep snow.

children.name: Urocyon
children.description: Gray foxes are small to medium-sized canids that are uniquely adapted for climbing trees, making them the most arboreal members of the dog family. They have grizzled gray fur with rusty-red sides and a distinctive black stripe running down their tail. These foxes are primarily nocturnal and are excellent hunters of small mammals, birds, and insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other North American foxes, gray foxes have semi-retractable claws and strong, flexible limbs that allow them to climb trees like cats. Their grizzled gray coloration and black-tipped tail also set them apart from the more reddish coloration of red foxes.
children.funFact: Gray foxes are the only members of the dog family in North America that can truly climb trees, often sleeping in tree hollows up to 30 feet above the ground and using their climbing ability to escape predators and access food sources like bird eggs and fruit.

children.description: Canids are the dog family, including wolves, domestic dogs, foxes, and coyotes. These intelligent carnivores are built for hunting with long legs, keen senses, and powerful jaws filled with sharp teeth. Most canids are social animals that communicate through howls, barks, and scent marking.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Canids have elongated snouts, upright triangular ears, and non-retractable claws unlike cats. They typically have bushy tails and walk on their toes (digitigrade), giving them speed and agility for chasing prey.
children.funFact: All domestic dog breeds, from tiny Chihuahuas to massive Great Danes, belong to the same species as gray wolves and can still interbreed with them.

children.name: Felidae
Lynx
children.description: Lynxes are medium-sized wild cats known for their distinctive tufted ears, short black-tipped tails, and large padded paws that act like snowshoes. These solitary hunters are perfectly adapted for life in forests and snowy environments, with excellent hearing and vision for tracking prey. In New England, you might encounter the smaller bobcat or the larger, more northern Canada lynx.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lynxes can be distinguished from other wild cats by their prominent ear tufts, facial ruffs that frame their faces like a beard, and relatively short tails with black tips. Their oversized paws are much larger than those of domestic cats or other small predators.
children.funFact: A lynx's hearing is so acute that it can detect a mouse moving under 2 feet of snow from 60 feet away.

children.name: Felis
children.description: The genus Felis includes small wild cats from Europe, Africa, and Asia, along with our familiar domestic cat. These are compact, agile hunters with retractable claws, excellent night vision, and flexible spines that allow them to squeeze through tight spaces and land on their feet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike larger cats, Felis species can purr continuously while breathing in and out, but they cannot roar. They're also smaller and more lightly built than other cat genera, typically weighing under 20 pounds.
children.funFact: Domestic cats share about 95% of their DNA with tigers, yet they're one of the few cat species that chose to live alongside humans rather than being domesticated by force.

children.name: Puma
children.description: The genus Puma contains large, powerful cats known for their incredible athletic abilities and adaptability to diverse habitats. These solitary predators are characterized by their muscular build, long tail, and uniform coat coloration that ranges from tawny to grayish-brown. Mountain lions are apex predators that can leap vertically up to 15 feet and horizontally up to 40 feet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other large cats, mountain lions cannot roar due to the structure of their throat bones, instead communicating through chirps, whistles, and screams. They are distinguished from other big cats by their relatively small head, long tail that's about one-third of their body length, and their ability to purr.
children.funFact: Mountain lions have the largest geographic range of any native terrestrial mammal in the Western Hemisphere, historically found from Canada to the southern tip of South America.

children.description: Felids are the cat family, including everything from your house cat to lions and tigers. All members of this family are carnivorous hunters with retractable claws, excellent night vision, and flexible bodies built for stalking and pouncing on prey. They are solitary animals (except for lions) with keen senses and powerful jaw muscles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other carnivores, felids have retractable claws that stay sharp for climbing and catching prey, and they have a specialized rough tongue covered in tiny hooks called papillae for grooming and scraping meat from bones.
children.funFact: All cats, from tiny house cats to massive tigers, cannot taste sweetness because they lack the genetic ability to detect sugar - they're such specialized meat-eaters that they evolved without needing to identify sweet foods.

children.name: Phocidae
Halichoerus
children.description: Grey seals are large marine mammals that represent the only species in their genus found in New England waters. These robust seals are excellent swimmers and divers, spending most of their time in the ocean but coming ashore to rest, mate, and give birth to their pups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grey seals can be distinguished from other seal species by their elongated snouts and larger size, with males being significantly bigger than females and sporting distinctive saggy neck rolls.
children.funFact: Grey seal pups are born with fluffy white coats that they molt within their first few weeks of life, and they can hold their breath for up to 70 minutes while diving for fish.

children.name: Phoca
children.description: Common seals, belonging to the genus Phoca, are true seals that spend time both in water and on land. They are medium-sized marine mammals with streamlined bodies perfectly adapted for swimming and diving. These seals are known for their docile nature and curious behavior around humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike sea lions, common seals cannot rotate their rear flippers forward, so they must wiggle on their bellies when moving on land. They have relatively small front flippers compared to other seal species and lack external ear flaps.
children.funFact: Harbor seals can hold their breath for up to 30 minutes and dive as deep as 1,500 feet while hunting for fish, though they typically prefer shallow coastal waters.

children.name: Pagophilus
children.description: Harp Seals are medium-sized marine mammals that spend most of their lives in the cold waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. They are highly migratory seals that travel thousands of miles between their feeding and breeding areas, following the seasonal ice patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Harp Seals are easily recognized by their distinctive black harp or saddle-shaped markings on their backs and sides, which develop as they mature from their famous white pup coats.
children.funFact: Baby harp seals are born with fluffy white fur and bright blue eyes, but they can only nurse for about 12 days before their mothers abandon them to fend for themselves on the ice.

children.name: Cystophora
children.description: Hooded seals are large, ice-loving seals that spend most of their lives in the frigid waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic Ocean. They are excellent deep divers, capable of reaching depths over 3,000 feet while hunting for fish and squid in the dark ocean depths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male hooded seals are easily recognized by their inflatable nasal sac that looks like a red balloon when expanded, which gives them their name. They are also much larger than most other seal species, with males weighing up to 900 pounds.
children.funFact: Baby hooded seals have the shortest nursing period of any mammal - mothers nurse their pups for only 4 days, during which the pups gain about 15 pounds per day!

children.description: Earless seals are marine mammals that are perfectly adapted for life in the ocean, spending most of their time underwater hunting for fish and coming ashore only to rest, mate, and give birth. Unlike their sea lion cousins, these seals have streamlined bodies with no external ear flaps and short front flippers that make them incredibly efficient swimmers but awkward on land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These seals lack external ears and have rear flippers that cannot rotate forward, so they must wiggle on their bellies when moving on land rather than walking on all fours like sea lions.
children.funFact: Harbor seals can hold their breath for up to 30 minutes and dive as deep as 1,500 feet while hunting, using their sensitive whiskers to detect vibrations from fish swimming nearby even in murky water.

children.name: Procyonidae
Procyon
children.description: Raccoons are medium-sized mammals known for their distinctive black facial masks and ringed tails. They are highly adaptable omnivores with dexterous front paws that they use almost like hands to manipulate objects and food. These intelligent creatures are primarily nocturnal and excellent climbers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Raccoons can be distinguished from other mammals by their unique black 'bandit mask' around their eyes and their bushy tail with dark rings. Their front paws are extremely nimble and sensitive, allowing them to feel and grasp objects with remarkable dexterity.
children.funFact: Raccoons don't actually 'wash' their food as commonly believed - they wet their paws to enhance their sense of touch, which helps them better examine and identify what they're about to eat.

children.description: The Procyonidae family includes medium-sized mammals known for their dexterous front paws, masked facial markings, and omnivorous diets. These intelligent animals are excellent climbers and are famous for their ability to manipulate objects with their highly sensitive hands. Most species have distinctive ringed tails and are active primarily at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other carnivores, procyonids have highly developed tactile abilities in their front paws, which they often use to examine food underwater. Their facial masks and ringed tails are also distinctive features that separate them from related carnivore families.
children.funFact: Raccoons don't actually "wash" their food - they're using their incredibly sensitive paws to gather more information about what they're eating, and water enhances their sense of touch!

children.name: Ursidae
Ursus
children.description: Holarctic Bears (Ursus) are the true bears found across the northern regions of North America and Eurasia. These large, powerful mammals are characterized by their stocky build, rounded ears, and plantigrade feet (walking on the soles of their feet like humans do). They are omnivores with excellent senses of smell and hearing, and most species can climb trees when young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bear families, Ursus bears have relatively short tails, non-retractable claws, and distinctive facial profiles with elongated snouts. They also have a more varied diet compared to more specialized bears like the bamboo-eating Giant Panda.
children.funFact: Despite their massive size and fearsome reputation, American Black Bears are excellent swimmers and can run up to 35 miles per hour – faster than any human!

children.description: Bears are large, powerful mammals with stocky builds, thick fur, and strong claws. They are omnivores that eat everything from berries and fish to small mammals, and most species can stand upright on their hind legs. Bears have excellent senses of smell and hearing, which help them find food and detect danger.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bears are much larger and more robust than other carnivores, with distinctive rounded ears, short tails, and a lumbering gait. Unlike cats or dogs, bears walk on the soles of their feet (plantigrade) rather than on their toes.
children.funFact: Despite their bulky appearance, bears can run up to 35 miles per hour and are surprisingly good swimmers and climbers.

children.name: Mephitidae
Mephitis
children.description: The genus Mephitis includes the classic black-and-white skunks that most people recognize. These medium-sized mammals are famous for their ability to spray a strong-smelling liquid when threatened, and they all share the distinctive pattern of white stripes or patches on black fur.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mephitis are larger than spotted skunks and have longer, bushier tails that they raise like a warning flag when threatened. Their spray apparatus is more developed than other skunk genera, making them the most potent of all skunks.
children.funFact: Striped skunks can accurately spray their defensive musk up to 10 feet away, and before spraying, they'll often do a handstand to make themselves look bigger and more intimidating!

children.description: Skunks and stink-badgers are small to medium-sized mammals famous for their ability to spray a powerful, foul-smelling liquid when threatened. These black and white striped or spotted animals are omnivores that feed on insects, small mammals, eggs, and plant matter. They have strong claws for digging and are most active during twilight and nighttime hours.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets this family apart is their specialized anal scent glands that can accurately spray a sulfur-rich musk up to 10 feet away. Unlike other carnivores, they also have a distinctive warning behavior of stamping their feet and raising their tails before spraying.
children.funFact: A skunk can spray its musk up to six times before needing to replenish its supply, which takes about 10 days to fully regenerate.

children.description: Carnivorans are an order of mammals that includes some of our most familiar predators like cats, dogs, bears, and seals. While their name suggests they all eat meat, many species are actually omnivores that enjoy both plants and animals, and some (like giant pandas) are primarily plant-eaters. What unites them is their shared evolutionary history and certain anatomical features rather than their diet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Carnivorans typically have specialized teeth called carnassials that act like scissors for slicing meat, along with well-developed canine teeth. Most also have retractable or semi-retractable claws and excellent senses for hunting.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'carnivorans,' some members like bears can be mostly vegetarian - black bears' diets are often 85% plant matter!

children.name: Rodentia
Cricetidae
Peromyscus
children.description: North American deer mice are small, agile rodents with large eyes, prominent ears, and long tails that are typically dark on top and white underneath. These nocturnal creatures are excellent climbers and jumpers, making their homes in forests, fields, and sometimes buildings throughout New England. They're known for their soft, dense fur and distinctive white feet and bellies that contrast with their brown or gray backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Deer mice can be distinguished from other small rodents by their bi-colored tails (dark above, white below) and their distinctly white feet and undersides. Unlike house mice, they have larger eyes and ears relative to their body size, and their fur is much softer and cleaner-looking.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, deer mice are incredible athletes that can leap up to 8 feet horizontally and climb nearly vertical surfaces using their semi-retractable claws.

children.name: Microtus
children.description: Meadow voles are small, stocky rodents with short tails and dense brown fur that live in grasslands, meadows, and forest floors throughout New England. These busy little mammals are active year-round, creating extensive runway systems through grass and vegetation as they search for food. They're herbivores that feed primarily on grasses, seeds, roots, and bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike mice, meadow voles have much shorter tails (less than half their body length), smaller ears, and blunter snouts. They're also more robust and stocky compared to the slender build of most mice and shrews.
children.funFact: A single meadow vole can eat its own body weight in vegetation every day and create runway systems with over 100 feet of interconnected trails!

children.name: Ondatra
children.description: Common muskrats are semi-aquatic rodents that live in wetlands, marshes, and along waterways throughout North America. They are medium-sized mammals with dense, waterproof fur and specialized adaptations for life both in water and on land. These industrious animals are known for building dome-shaped lodges and extensive burrow systems in their aquatic habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Muskrats can be distinguished from other aquatic rodents by their distinctive laterally flattened tail that acts like a rudder, and their partially webbed hind feet. They are much smaller than beavers but larger than voles, with prominent orange front teeth adapted for gnawing vegetation.
children.funFact: Muskrats got their name from the musky scent they produce from special glands, which they use to mark their territory and communicate with other muskrats.

children.name: Clethrionomys
children.description: Red-backed voles are small, stocky rodents that live in the cool, moist forests of northern regions. They are characterized by their distinctive reddish-brown stripe running down their back, which contrasts with their grayish sides and white belly. These active little mammals are excellent climbers and spend much of their time foraging both on the ground and in trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Red-backed voles can be distinguished from other small rodents by their prominent rusty-red dorsal stripe and their relatively short tail that's less than half their body length. Unlike meadow voles, they have larger ears and eyes, and their fur is much more colorful.
children.funFact: Red-backed voles are one of the few small mammals that remain active throughout winter, creating elaborate tunnel systems under the snow where they continue to forage for seeds, bark, and fungi.

children.name: Synaptomys
children.description: Synaptomys is a small genus of voles commonly known as bog lemmings, specialized for life in wet, marshy habitats. These small rodents are distinguished by their short tails, small ears, and dense fur that helps them survive in cold, damp environments. They are herbivorous mammals that feed primarily on grasses, sedges, and mosses found in their boggy homes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bog lemmings can be distinguished from other voles by their notably short tails (less than 25% of their body length) and grooved upper incisors. They also have smaller eyes and ears compared to meadow voles, reflecting their more secretive lifestyle in dense vegetation.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bog lemmings,' these animals don't actually migrate in large groups like true lemmings - they're actually more closely related to voles and got their common name simply because of their small size and northern distribution.

children.description: This diverse family of small rodents includes some of New England's most common mammals, from the tiny deer mice that might visit your bird feeder to the semi-aquatic muskrats building lodges in wetlands. All members share similar dental features with ever-growing teeth adapted for gnawing plant material, and most have compact bodies with relatively short tails compared to rats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true rats and mice (Muridae), cricetids typically have shorter tails, more robust builds, and specialized cheek teeth with distinct cusps arranged in triangular patterns for grinding vegetation.
children.funFact: Lemmings, famous for their population cycles, don't actually commit mass suicide by jumping off cliffs - this myth likely comes from their dramatic population booms that force them to disperse into unfamiliar territory where some may accidentally fall.

children.name: Sciuridae
Glaucomys
children.description: New World Flying Squirrels are small, nocturnal mammals with a remarkable ability to glide through the forest canopy. They have a furry membrane called a patagium that stretches between their front and back legs, allowing them to soar from tree to tree rather than truly fly. These agile creatures are perfectly adapted for life in the treetops, with large eyes for night vision and soft fur that helps them move silently.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other squirrels, flying squirrels have a gliding membrane and flattened tail that acts as a rudder during flight. They are also strictly nocturnal, while most other squirrels are active during the day.
children.funFact: Flying squirrels can glide over 150 feet in a single leap and are so quiet that you might never know they're living in your backyard!

children.name: Sciurus
children.description: Tree squirrels in the genus Sciurus are medium-sized rodents perfectly adapted for life in the trees. They have bushy tails that help with balance and communication, strong claws for gripping bark, and excellent jumping abilities that allow them to leap between branches with remarkable agility.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ground squirrels or flying squirrels, Sciurus species are primarily arboreal and have proportionally longer tails and more robust limbs for climbing. Their tails are particularly fluffy and serve multiple purposes beyond just balance.
children.funFact: Tree squirrels can rotate their hind feet 180 degrees, allowing them to run headfirst down tree trunks with their back claws providing the grip.

children.name: Tamias
children.description: The genus Tamias contains the true chipmunks of North America, small ground-dwelling squirrels known for their distinctive striped patterns and cheek pouches. These energetic rodents are expert foragers that collect and store nuts, seeds, and other food items in underground burrows. They're distinguished by their compact size, typically measuring 8-10 inches long plus a bushy tail.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other squirrels, Tamias chipmunks have prominent facial stripes that extend through the eye area and large internal cheek pouches that can expand to three times the size of their head. They also have a more terrestrial lifestyle compared to tree squirrels, spending most of their time on or near the ground.
children.funFact: Eastern chipmunks can stuff up to 32 beechnuts in their expandable cheek pouches at one time, allowing them to efficiently transport large quantities of food back to their burrows for winter storage.

children.name: Tamiasciurus
children.description: Pine squirrels are small, energetic tree squirrels that specialize in living in coniferous forests. They are expert climbers and spend most of their time in the trees, where they build their nests and gather food. These squirrels are known for their territorial behavior and their impressive ability to store large quantities of seeds and nuts for winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pine squirrels are smaller than gray squirrels and have tufted ears, especially prominent in winter. They have a distinctive rusty-red coat and a white belly, along with a much more aggressive and territorial personality than other squirrel species.
children.funFact: A single pine squirrel can collect and store up to 18,000 spruce cones in underground caches called middens, which can grow to be 30 feet across and several feet deep over many generations of squirrels using the same site.

children.name: Marmota
children.description: Marmots are large, stocky ground squirrels that are well-adapted for life in burrows. These social rodents are known for their ability to hibernate through winter months and their loud whistling alarm calls that warn others of danger.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Marmots are much larger and more robust than other squirrels, with powerful claws for digging extensive burrow systems. Unlike tree squirrels, they spend most of their time on or under the ground.
children.funFact: Groundhogs can whistle through their teeth to communicate with other marmots, and despite their common name, they're actually more closely related to squirrels than to hogs.

children.description: Squirrels are agile, bushy-tailed rodents that have adapted to life in trees, underground burrows, and everywhere in between. All members of this family share strong hind legs for jumping, sharp claws for climbing, and large front teeth that grow continuously throughout their lives for gnawing nuts, seeds, and bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other rodents, squirrels have particularly well-developed spatial memory and demonstrate complex food-caching behaviors. Their distinctive bushy tails serve multiple purposes including balance while climbing, communication through tail movements, and insulation during cold weather.
children.funFact: A gray squirrel can remember the locations of thousands of buried nuts and can find them even under a foot of snow months later.

children.name: Muridae
Rattus
children.description: Old World Rats are a genus of medium-sized rodents that originated in Asia but have spread worldwide through human activity. These adaptable mammals are characterized by their long, scaly tails, pointed snouts, and excellent climbing and swimming abilities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Old World Rats can be distinguished from native New England rodents by their larger size, longer tails (usually longer than their body), and more robust build compared to native mice and voles.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Norway rats,' Brown Rats actually originated in northern China and didn't reach Norway until the 1700s - they just happened to arrive in England on Norwegian ships!

children.name: Mus
children.description: Typical Old World Mice are small rodents in the genus Mus that originally evolved in Asia and spread across much of the world. These mice are characterized by their pointed snouts, large ears, long tails, and small size, typically weighing less than an ounce. They are highly adaptable creatures that have successfully colonized diverse habitats worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike New World mice and voles, Mus species have longer, more sparsely haired tails and tend to be smaller overall. They also have a distinctive musky odor and different dental patterns compared to native North American rodents.
children.funFact: House mice can produce up to 10 litters per year with 4-8 babies each, and young mice can start reproducing when they're only 6 weeks old, making them one of the most prolific mammals on Earth.

children.name: Meriones
children.description: Jirds are small, desert-adapted rodents in the gerbil family known for their long tails and excellent jumping abilities. These social animals have specialized kidneys that allow them to conserve water efficiently, making them well-suited for arid environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jirds can be distinguished from other small rodents by their long, furry tails that are often longer than their bodies, and their powerful hind legs adapted for hopping and jumping.
children.funFact: Mongolian jirds communicate through foot drumming, rapidly thumping their hind feet on the ground to send vibrations that can be felt by other jirds up to several feet away.

children.description: Old World Mice and Rats are a large family of small rodents that originally came from Europe, Asia, and Africa. These animals are characterized by their long, scaly tails, pointed snouts, and large ears, and they're excellent at adapting to life around humans. Most species are opportunistic omnivores that will eat seeds, grains, fruits, and even small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their New World cousins, Old World mice and rats have distinctive tuberculate molars (with rounded bumps) rather than prismatic teeth, and their tails are typically longer relative to their body size.
children.funFact: The house mouse can squeeze through openings as small as a dime, and Norway rats are such good swimmers they can tread water for up to three days!

children.name: Zapodidae
Zapus
children.description: Zapus is a genus of small rodents known as meadow jumping mice, characterized by their incredibly long hind legs and tail that help them make spectacular leaps through grasslands and meadows. These tiny acrobats are built for bouncing, with powerful leg muscles that allow them to jump distances many times their body length when startled or moving quickly through their habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Zapus can be distinguished from other jumping mice by their shorter ears, brownish coloration with darker back stripes, and their preference for moist meadow habitats rather than dry areas.
children.funFact: Northern meadow jumping mice can leap up to 8 feet in a single bound - that's like a human jumping nearly 50 feet!

children.name: Napaeozapus
children.description: Woodland jumping mice are small forest rodents known for their remarkable jumping ability and extremely long tails. These mice are specialized for life in cool, moist woodlands where they feed primarily on fungi, seeds, and berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jumping mice, woodland jumping mice have distinctive white-tipped tails and prefer deep forest habitats rather than grasslands or meadows.
children.funFact: Woodland jumping mice can leap up to 12 feet in a single bound when escaping predators, using their incredibly long tail as a balancing rudder during flight.

children.description: Jumping mice are small rodents with extremely long hind legs and tails that can leap impressive distances when startled or moving quickly. These nocturnal mice are excellent jumpers, using their powerful back legs to bound through grasslands, meadows, and forest edges in search of seeds and other food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their exceptionally long hind legs and tails (often longer than their body) set them apart from other small rodents, giving them their characteristic hopping locomotion rather than typical scurrying movement.
children.funFact: Jumping mice can leap up to 8 feet in a single bound - that's like a human jumping nearly 50 feet!

children.name: Castoridae
Castor
children.description: Beavers are large, semi-aquatic rodents known for their remarkable engineering abilities and distinctive flat, paddle-shaped tails. These industrious mammals are perfectly adapted for life both in water and on land, with waterproof fur, webbed hind feet, and powerful teeth for cutting down trees. They are ecosystem engineers that dramatically modify their environment by building dams, lodges, and canals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beavers are distinguished from other rodents by their massive size (they're the second-largest rodents in the world), their unique flat, scaly tail, and their prominent orange-colored front teeth. Their combination of aquatic adaptations and tree-felling abilities is unmatched among North American mammals.
children.funFact: A beaver's teeth never stop growing throughout their lifetime, and the orange color comes from iron in the enamel, which actually helps make them stronger for gnawing through wood.

children.description: Beavers are large, semi-aquatic rodents known for their impressive engineering abilities and distinctive flat, paddle-shaped tails. They are herbivores that spend much of their time in and around water, building dams and lodges from wood, mud, and stones. These industrious mammals are perfectly adapted for life both in water and on land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beavers are easily recognized by their large, flat, scaly tails, webbed hind feet, and prominent orange front teeth that never stop growing. Unlike other rodents, they have dense, waterproof fur and can close their ears and nostrils when diving underwater.
children.funFact: A beaver's teeth are orange because they contain iron, which makes them incredibly strong and perfect for gnawing through tree trunks up to several feet thick.

children.name: Erethizontidae
Erethizon
children.description: Erethizon is a genus containing the North American porcupine, one of the most distinctive mammals in our region. These large rodents are famous for their impressive coat of sharp, barbed quills that serve as their primary defense against predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike Old World porcupines found in Africa and Asia, North American porcupines are excellent climbers with strong claws and are the only porcupines in the Americas that spend significant time in trees.
children.funFact: A single North American porcupine has around 30,000 quills, and contrary to popular belief, they cannot shoot their quills but rather release them easily when touched by a predator.

children.description: New World Porcupines are large, slow-moving rodents famous for their defensive coat of sharp, barbed quills. Unlike their Old World cousins, these porcupines are excellent climbers with strong claws and partially prehensile tails that help them navigate tree branches. They are herbivorous mammals that feed primarily on bark, twigs, and other plant materials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: New World Porcupines differ from Old World porcupines by being arboreal (tree-dwelling) rather than ground-dwelling, and they have longer, more flexible quills. They also possess partially prehensile tails and are generally smaller in size.
children.funFact: A single porcupine can have up to 30,000 quills covering its body, and contrary to popular belief, they cannot shoot their quills but rather release them when touched or threatened.

children.description: Rodents are the largest group of mammals in the world, united by their continuously growing front teeth that they use for gnawing. These adaptable creatures have conquered nearly every habitat on Earth, from underground burrows to treetops to wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: All rodents have a pair of ever-growing incisors (front teeth) in both upper and lower jaws that are kept sharp and properly sized through constant gnawing. Unlike rabbits, which also have prominent front teeth, rodents have only one pair of incisors in each jaw.
children.funFact: A rodent's teeth never stop growing throughout its entire life - if they didn't gnaw constantly to wear them down, their teeth would eventually grow so long they couldn't eat!

children.name: Eulipotyphla
Soricidae
Sorex
children.description: Long-tailed shrews are tiny, mouse-like mammals with pointed snouts and incredibly high metabolisms. These energetic hunters must eat almost constantly throughout the day and night, consuming insects, spiders, and other small prey to fuel their rapid heartbeats and breathing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their short-tailed shrew cousins, these shrews have tails that are at least half the length of their body. They also lack the venomous bite that short-tailed shrews possess.
children.funFact: The American Pygmy Shrew is one of the smallest mammals in North America, weighing less than a dime and needing to eat every few hours or it will starve to death.

children.name: Blarina
children.description: Short-tailed shrews are small, velvety-furred mammals with notably short tails and tiny eyes that spend most of their lives underground or in dense vegetation. They are incredibly active predators that must eat almost constantly to fuel their extremely high metabolism, consuming insects, worms, and even small vertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other shrews, short-tailed shrews have proportionally shorter tails and are notably larger and more robust. They also have venomous saliva that helps them subdue prey larger than themselves.
children.funFact: Short-tailed shrews are among the few venomous mammals in North America - their saliva contains toxins that can paralyze prey as large as mice and frogs.

children.name: Cryptotis
children.description: Small-eared shrews are tiny, mouse-sized mammals with incredibly high metabolisms that must eat constantly to survive. These diminutive predators have velvety fur, pointed snouts, and tiny eyes and ears that give them their name. They spend their lives hunting insects, spiders, and other small prey both above and below ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Small-eared shrews can be distinguished from other shrews by their proportionally smaller ears and eyes, plus their relatively short tails. They also have distinctive dental features with red-tipped teeth that help identify them from similar species.
children.funFact: Small-eared shrews have such fast metabolisms that they must eat every 2-3 hours or they will starve to death, consuming up to three times their body weight in food each day.

children.description: Shrews are tiny, mouse-like mammals with incredibly high metabolisms that must eat almost constantly to survive. These energetic little creatures have pointed snouts, small eyes, and dense velvety fur that helps them navigate through leaf litter and underground tunnels. Despite their small size, they are fierce predators that hunt insects, worms, and other small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike mice and other small rodents, shrews have sharp, pointed teeth designed for eating meat rather than gnawing, and they produce a musky scent from special glands. Their snouts are much more elongated and flexible than those of rodents, helping them probe for prey in tight spaces.
children.funFact: Some New England shrews have venomous saliva that helps paralyze their prey - they're among the few venomous mammals in the world!

children.name: Talpidae
Parascalops
children.description: Parascalops is a genus containing just one species - the Hairy-tailed Mole found in eastern North America. These are small, underground mammals perfectly adapted for a life of digging through soil in search of earthworms, grubs, and other invertebrates. They have powerful front claws, tiny eyes, and velvety fur that can lay flat in any direction as they move through their tunnels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The Hairy-tailed Mole is distinguished from other North American moles by its distinctly hairy tail, which is about one-third the length of its body and covered in coarse black hairs.
children.funFact: Despite living almost entirely underground, Hairy-tailed Moles are excellent swimmers and will sometimes tunnel right under streams, emerging to swim across when their underground routes are blocked.

children.name: Condylura
children.description: Condylura is a genus containing just one remarkable species - the star-nosed mole. This small mammal is perfectly adapted for life underground and in wet environments, spending most of its time tunneling through soil and swimming in streams and ponds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining characteristic of this genus is the extraordinary star-shaped nose appendage made up of 22 fleshy rays that function as an incredibly sensitive touch organ.
children.funFact: The star-nosed mole has the fastest-known foraging speed of any mammal, able to identify and consume small prey in as little as 120 milliseconds.

children.name: Scalopus
children.description: Scalopus is a genus of small, underground mammals known as moles that spend almost their entire lives tunneling through soil. These highly specialized diggers have powerful front limbs with large claws, tiny eyes, and soft, velvety fur that can lie flat in any direction as they move through their tunnels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scalopus moles are distinguished from other North American moles by their larger size, broader front feet, and lack of a visible tail above ground.
children.funFact: A single Eastern Mole can dig up to 18 feet of tunnel in just one hour, creating an extensive underground highway system for hunting earthworms and insects.

children.description: Moles and desmans are small mammals perfectly adapted for life underground, with powerful front paws for digging and cylindrical bodies that slip easily through tunnels. These insectivores spend most of their lives beneath the surface, creating extensive tunnel systems as they hunt for earthworms, grubs, and other soil-dwelling prey. Their soft, velvety fur can lie flat in any direction, allowing them to move forward or backward through tight spaces with equal ease.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small mammals, moles have enormous front paws with long claws for digging, tiny eyes that are often hidden by fur, and no external ears. Their snouts are highly sensitive and specialized for detecting prey in complete darkness underground.
children.funFact: A single mole can dig up to 150 feet of tunnels in just one day, and their tunnels can extend over an acre of underground territory!

children.description: Eulipotyphla includes some of the world's smallest mammals, united by their insect-eating lifestyle and distinctive pointed snouts. These tiny powerhouses have incredibly high metabolisms and must eat almost constantly to survive, consuming their body weight in insects, worms, and other invertebrates daily.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike rodents which they're sometimes confused with, eulipotyphlans have sharp, pointed teeth designed for piercing insect shells rather than gnawing. They also lack the enlarged front teeth (incisors) that characterize rodents.
children.funFact: Shrews have such fast metabolisms that they can starve to death in just a few hours without food - their hearts can beat over 1,000 times per minute!

children.name: Chiroptera
Vespertilionidae
Myotis
children.description: Mouse-eared bats are a diverse group of small, insect-eating bats that get their name from their prominent, mouse-like ears. These nocturnal creatures are excellent fliers that use echolocation to navigate and hunt for insects in the dark. All members of this group are found throughout New England's forests, caves, and human structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mouse-eared bats can be distinguished from other bat groups by their relatively large ears, small size, and brown fur coloration. Their ears are typically longer than they are wide, giving them their characteristic mouse-like appearance.
children.funFact: A single Little Brown Bat can catch over 1,000 mosquitoes in just one hour of hunting, making them incredibly valuable natural pest controllers.

children.name: Lasiurus
children.description: Hairy-tailed bats are medium-sized bats known for their distinctively furry tail membranes, which are covered in dense hair rather than being bare like most other bat species. These solitary bats are excellent long-distance fliers and are among the few bat species that migrate seasonally rather than hibernating in caves or buildings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other bats, hairy-tailed bats have thick fur covering their tail membranes, giving them their common name. They also tend to roost alone in trees rather than forming large colonies in caves or structures.
children.funFact: Hairy-tailed bats can migrate over 1,000 miles between their summer and winter ranges, with some individuals traveling from Canada all the way to Mexico!

children.name: Eptesicus
children.description: House bats are medium to large-sized bats that are often found roosting in and around human structures like attics, barns, and bridges. They are strong fliers with broad wings and are known for their adaptability to urban and suburban environments. These bats are insectivores that hunt for flying insects during twilight and nighttime hours.
children.distinguishingFeatures: House bats are typically larger and more robust than many other bat species, with broad, rounded ears and relatively slow, steady flight patterns. They have thick, dense fur and are less agile in flight compared to smaller bat species, but make up for it with endurance and strength.
children.funFact: Big brown bats can live over 30 years and have been recorded flying at altitudes up to 9,000 feet, making them some of the highest-flying bats in North America.

children.name: Lasionycteris
children.description: Lasionycteris is a genus containing just one species of bat - the Silver-haired Bat. These medium-sized bats are known for their distinctive dark fur with silver-tipped hairs that give them their characteristic frosted appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Silver-haired bats are easily distinguished from other New England bats by their unique silver-frosted dark fur and their preference for roosting in tree bark rather than caves or buildings.
children.funFact: Silver-haired bats are long-distance migrants that can travel over 1,000 miles between their summer and winter habitats, making them one of the most migratory bat species in North America.

children.name: Perimyotis
children.description: Perimyotis is a small genus of bats that contains just one species in New England - the Tricolored Bat. These are tiny insect-eating bats that are among the smallest bat species found in North America. They get their name from their distinctive tri-colored fur pattern.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Perimyotis bats are distinguished by their extremely small size and their unique fur coloration where individual hairs have three distinct color bands - dark at the base, light in the middle, and dark at the tip.
children.funFact: The Tricolored Bat is one of the smallest bats in North America, weighing only about as much as a penny and small enough to fit in a large thimble.

children.description: Evening bats are the most common and widespread family of bats found throughout New England. These small to medium-sized bats are excellent fliers that hunt insects at night using echolocation, with most species becoming active around dusk.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike some other bat families, evening bats have simple, unadorned noses without elaborate leaf-like structures, and their ears are typically moderate in size with a small pointed tragus (ear flap).
children.funFact: The little brown bat, a member of this family, can catch up to 1,000 mosquito-sized insects in a single hour while hunting at night.

children.description: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, using wings made of stretched skin membranes between elongated finger bones. These nocturnal creatures have evolved sophisticated echolocation abilities, allowing them to navigate and hunt insects in complete darkness by emitting high-frequency sounds and interpreting the echoes.
